headings: Ruling 6: Handwritten notes produced by Southern Steel
paragraphs.text: The respondents did not contend that the above Salesforce record was inadmissible.

headings: Ruling 6: Handwritten notes produced by Southern Steel
Ruling 6: Handwritten notes produced by Southern Steel
paragraphs.text: The respondents referred me to a second Salesforce record created by Mr Sparks on 17 December 2013 which relates to a telephone call between Mr Sparks and Jim Larkin of Southern Steel. The respondents submitted that that record suggests that the handwritten notes might have been created by Mr Larkin and not by Mr Lander. I note, however, that the second Salesforce record referred to by the respondents records that the telephone call between Mr Sparks and Mr Larkin occurred on 17 September 2013, not 16 September 2013. The handwritten note bears the latter date.

headings: Ruling 6: Handwritten notes produced by Southern Steel
paragraphs.text: Based on the foregoing, I am satisfied that the two handwritten notes were authored by Mr Lander of Brice Metals. In respect of the note bearing the date 16 September 2013, I am satisfied that the note records statements made during a telephone call between Mr Sparks and Mr Lander made on that date. I am also satisfied that, for the most part, the note records matters communicated by Mr Sparks to Mr Lander, being BlueScope’s proposed price list in respect of flat steel products and matters related to the price list. That conclusion is consistent with Mr Hennessy’s evidence, Mr Sparks’ record of the conversation to the effect that they discussed BlueScope’s pricing position and the content of Mr Lander’s note.

headings: Ruling 6: Handwritten notes produced by Southern Steel
paragraphs.text: In respect of the note bearing the date 4 February 2014, I am satisfied that it also records a conversation between Mr Sparks and Mr Lander. I have not been taken to any other evidence that establishes whether the conversation occurred in person or over a telecommunications device. Despite that, I am satisfied from the content of the note that the subject matter concerns BlueScope’s pricing for flat steel products which was communicated by Mr Sparks to Mr Lander on that day. That conclusion is reinforced by the fact that, on 5 February 2014, BlueScope provided Southern Steel with formal notification of its price list (designated as recommended resale prices) for sheet and coil products for April 2014.

headings: Ruling 6: Handwritten notes produced by Southern Steel
paragraphs.text: Having regard to those matters, I am satisfied that the two handwritten notes form part of the records kept by Southern Steel (or its subsidiary Brice Metals) in the course of its business for the purposes of s 69(1). The records of a business are the documents (or other means of holding information) by which activities of the business, including business operations, internal communications, and communications between the business and third parties, are recorded: Roach v Page (No 15) [2003] NSWSC 939 at [5] per Sperling J. The phrase “kept by” in s 69(1) means “retained or held”: Australian Securities and Investments Commission v Rich [2005] NSWSC 417; 191 FLR 385 (ASIC v Rich) at [190] per Austin J. I am also satisfied that the notes contain previous representations (being matters communicated by Mr Sparks) made or recorded in the document in the course of and for the purposes of Southern Steel’s business. It follows that the notes are documents to which s 69 applies, within the meaning of s 69(1).

headings: Ruling 6: Handwritten notes produced by Southern Steel
paragraphs.text: In respect of documents within s 69(1), the hearsay rule is excluded in respect of representations that satisfy s 69(2). As observed by the New South Wales Court of Appeal in Panayi v Deputy Commissioner of Taxation [2017] NSWCA 93; 319 FLR 228, whether particular representations satisfy the requirements of s 69(2) can only be answered by focussing on the particular representations and the facts asserted in them (see at [43]). There are two levels of representation made or recorded in the handwritten notes. The first representation is made by Mr Lander and is to the effect that Mr Sparks communicated certain matters to Mr Lander concerning BlueScope’s price list as recorded in the notes. I am satisfied that, in respect of that representation, Mr Lander had personal knowledge of the asserted fact (the communication from Mr Sparks) and that, as a result, the hearsay rule does not apply to that representation (as per s 69(2)(a)). The second level of representation is made by Mr Sparks and is to the effect of the matters recorded in the notes, specifically as to BlueScope’s commercial proposals with respect to its prices and the use of those prices by distributors. I am satisfied that the second level of representation was made by Mr Sparks and that Mr Sparks had or might reasonably be supposed to have had personal knowledge of the asserted facts or that Mr Sparks made the representations on the basis of information directly or indirectly supplied by a person who had or might reasonably be supposed to have had personal knowledge of the asserted facts. I consider that those conclusions can be safely drawn based on Mr Hennessy’s evidence and the fact that Mr Sparks was an employee of BlueScope with responsibility for making the relevant communications with Mr Lander about BlueScope’s price lists. It follows that the hearsay rule does not apply to the second level of representation.

headings: Ruling 6: Handwritten notes produced by Southern Steel
paragraphs.text: It follows, therefore, that the handwritten notes are not inadmissible by reason of the hearsay rule in respect of the foregoing representations.

headings: Ruling 6: Handwritten notes produced by Southern Steel
paragraphs.text: I note a concession made by the ACCC in the course of argument with respect to the first note. Despite the first note referring to “Matt” (which I infer is a reference to Mr Hennessy) and “Jason Ellis” (the second respondent), the ACCC does not seek to prove by the note that either Mr Ellis or Mr Hennessy gave instructions to Mr Sparks in relation to the matters communicated to Mr Lander. I understand, though, that the concession is limited to what may be inferred from the note itself. In other words, it remains open to the Court to conclude from other admissible evidence that Messrs Ellis and/or Hennessy gave relevant instructions to Mr Sparks.

headings: Ruling 6: Handwritten notes produced by Southern Steel
paragraphs.text: In respect of the relevance objection, the respondents submitted, in effect, that the handwritten notes were not sufficiently intelligible to be probative of any facts in the proceeding, and therefore the notes were irrelevant. In that respect, the respondents argued that all that was known about the notes is that they were produced by Southern Steel, and the author of the notes and the circumstances in which they were created is unknown. The respondents also argued that aspects of the notes were not legible. All in all, the respondents argued that giving meaning to the notes was an exercise in speculation.

headings: Ruling 6: Handwritten notes produced by Southern Steel
paragraphs.text: In my view, the respondents’ arguments on relevance lose their force once it has been established that the author of the notes is Mr Lander of Brice Metals and the notes record communications with Mr Sparks of BlueScope, as set out above. Further, while some words in the notes are not legible, the vast majority of the words are legible and have been set out above. In assessing the relevance of a document, the Court is permitted to examine it and may draw any reasonable inference from it (see s 58 of the Evidence Act).

headings: Ruling 6: Handwritten notes produced by Southern Steel
paragraphs.text: Having examined the notes, I consider that they have apparent relevance to the issues raised in the proceeding, as they involve a communication from BlueScope to a distributor of flat steel products concerning BlueScope’s forthcoming supply prices and changes in the approach to those prices, including reframing them as “recommended resale prices”. In respect of the note bearing the date 16 September 2013, it is directly relevant to proof of a fact alleged by the ACCC in its pleading, that on that date Mr Sparks of BlueScope had a conversation with Mr Lander of Southern Steel during which Mr Sparks said words to the effect that BlueScope would provide Southern Steel with a price list containing pricing information and the provision of that pricing information would provide participants in the market with the confidence to sell flat steel products in accordance with the pricing information. In respect of the note bearing the date 4 February 2014, I consider it has contextual relevance to the pleaded allegations.

headings: Ruling 6: Handwritten notes produced by Southern Steel
paragraphs.text:
Section 135 empowers the Court to exclude otherwise admissible evidence if its probative value is substantially outweighed by the danger that the evidence might be unfairly prejudicial to a party, might be misleading or confusing, or might cause or result in undue waste of time. Mr Ellis submitted that the Court should exclude the evidence in the case against him on the basis of unfair prejudice. In that respect, Mr Ellis argued that:
(a) he is an individual respondent in a civil penalty proceeding, which is a relevant consideration (referring to ASIC v Rich at [46]);
(b) there is no evidence to indicate that Mr Lander is unavailable to be called as a witness by the ACCC, and the Court should infer that the ACCC has made a forensic decision not to call Mr Lander which deprives Mr Ellis of the opportunity to cross-examine Mr Lander about the note; and
(c) the note itself has little if any probative value because of its unintelligibility.

headings: Ruling 6: Handwritten notes produced by Southern Steel
paragraphs.text: In response, the ACCC submitted that the mere fact that the ACCC does not intend to call Mr Lander, and that he is therefore unavailable for cross-examination, does not establish unfair prejudice. The ACCC further submitted that there is no property in a witness and BlueScope and Mr Ellis are not prevented from calling either Mr Sparks or Mr Lander as witnesses.

headings: Ruling 6: Handwritten notes produced by Southern Steel
paragraphs.text: For the reasons discussed above, I consider that the handwritten notes have probative value in the proceeding as direct proof of a pleaded allegation in the ACCC’s case. Thus, I would only exclude the notes if persuaded that their probative value is substantially outweighed by the danger that the evidence might be unfairly prejudicial to a party.

headings: Ruling 6: Handwritten notes produced by Southern Steel
paragraphs.text: It is trite to observe that evidence is not unfairly prejudicial to a party merely because it tends to damage the case of the party or support the case of an opponent: see Ainsworth v Burden [2005] NSWCA 174 at [99] per Hunt AJA (Handley and McColl JJA agreeing). Generally, the phrase refers to the risk that the evidence may be misused to make a factual finding otherwise than on a rational basis. However, it is accepted that unfair prejudice may arise from procedural considerations: see for example Galvin v The Queen [2006] NSWCCA 66; 161 A Crim R 449 at [40] per Howie J (McClellan CJ at CL and Latham J agreeing). Mr Ellis accepted that the admission of a business record as an exception to the hearsay rule, and the inability to cross-examine the author of the record, is not in and of itself unfair prejudice: see Papakosmas v The Queen (1999) 196 CLR 297 at [93] per McHugh J; Ordukaya v Hicks [2000] NSWCA 180 at [35]-[40] per Sheller JA (Meagher JA concurring). Nevertheless, a relevant consideration is whether the maker of the business record (or the representation contained within it) is available to give evidence. As observed by Sperling J in Roach v Page (No 11) [2003] NSWSC 907 at [74(g)], where the maker of the representation is available or is not shown to be unavailable and the party tendering the evidence does not call the person, that is a legitimate consideration in favour of a finding of unfair prejudice.

headings: Ruling 6: Handwritten notes produced by Southern Steel
paragraphs.text: I note that BlueScope does not seek the exclusion of the handwritten notes in the case against it under s 135. Even if such an application had been made, I would have rejected it. The alleged conversation between Mr Sparks and Mr Lander on 16 September 2013 is expressly relied on by the ACCC in respect of its pleaded case against BlueScope. The evidence indicates that Mr Sparks remains an employee of BlueScope. It is open to BlueScope to call Mr Sparks as a witness to give his account of the communications referred to in the notes. As a result, I do not consider that there is any danger that the evidence might be unfairly prejudicial to BlueScope.

headings: Ruling 6: Handwritten notes produced by Southern Steel
paragraphs.text: However, in the case of Mr Ellis, the balancing exercise required by s 135 raises different considerations. Mr Ellis is a separate respondent to the proceeding, facing separate (albeit overlapping) allegations to BlueScope and with separate legal representation. In its pleaded case against Mr Ellis, the ACCC does not allege that the conversation between Mr Sparks and Mr Lander on 16 September 2013 is an act to be attributed to Mr Ellis. Accordingly, the probative value of the conversation in the pleaded case against Mr Ellis is less direct than in the case of BlueScope. In relation to prejudice, I infer that Mr Ellis has no ability to compel Mr Sparks (or Mr Lander) to speak with him about the communications referred to in the notes. In my view, the ACCC’s submission that there is no property in a witness is not a complete answer to Mr Ellis’ arguments under s 135. It is the ACCC that seeks to tender and rely upon the handwritten notes, while choosing not to call as a witness the person shown by the evidence to be the author of the notes. In the circumstances, I consider that prejudice does arise to Mr Ellis in the circumstances on account of his inability to cross-examine Mr Lander. Further, I consider that the prejudice is unfair to Mr Ellis in circumstances where the ACCC has elected not to call the author of the note as a witness. Weighing the probative value of the handwritten notes in the case against Mr Ellis against the unfair prejudice, in my view the balance favours the exclusion of the notes in the case against Mr Ellis.

headings: Ruling 6: Handwritten notes produced by Southern Steel
paragraphs.text: Accordingly, I allowed the tender of the handwritten notes in the case against BlueScope, but not in the case against Mr Ellis. I reiterate that the handwritten notes are not, in any event, directly relied on by the ACCC in its pleaded case against Mr Ellis.

headings: Ruling 6: Handwritten notes produced by Southern Steel
paragraphs.text: The ACCC has liberty to revisit this ruling if either Mr Lander or Mr Sparks is called as a witness in the proceeding by any party, affording Mr Ellis an opportunity to test the evidence consisting of the representations contained in the handwritten notes.

As noted above, Mr Sparks remains an employee of BlueScope. The ACCC does not propose to call Mr Sparks as a witness in the proceeding, but sought to tender a number of representations made by Mr Sparks in two statements signed by him on 4 December 2017 and 7 July 2021 as admissions and context for those admissions pursuant to s 81 of the Evidence Act. In that regard, the ACCC submitted that Mr Sparks’ statements are to be taken to be an admission of BlueScope under s 87(1)(b). BlueScope did not advance a submission to the contrary. It was common ground between the parties that, by tendering Mr Sparks' statements as admissions, the statements would only be admissible in the ACCC's case against BlueScope and not the case against Mr Ellis.

BlueScope submitted that the course proposed by the ACCC in tendering Mr Sparks’ statements as admissions was highly unusual and that the Court should exercise its discretion to exclude the evidence under s 135 of the Evidence Act. BlueScope argued that the ACCC had obtained statements from Mr Sparks and, until very recently, the ACCC had indicated that it would call Mr Sparks as a witness. There is no evidence to suggest that Mr Sparks is unavailable to be called as a witness by the ACCC. Rather, BlueScope submitted, the ACCC had made a forensic decision to tender his statements as admissions rather than call him as a witness. The consequence of the decision is that BlueScope would lose the opportunity to cross-examine Mr Sparks on his statements. While it is open to BlueScope to call Mr Sparks as a witness, BlueScope would (at least in the first instance) be required to comply with the rules relating to examination-in-chief and the ACCC would be afforded the opportunity to cross-examine Mr Sparks. BlueScope submitted that this inverts the ordinary course of evidence, is without precedent and should not be encouraged. In circumstances where the ACCC has not brought forward any reason why Mr Sparks is not able to be called by it as a witness, BlueScope submitted that the Court ought to exclude Mr Sparks’ evidence under s 135 on the basis that it would cause prejudice to BlueScope to have it admitted in this way.

BlueScope’s submissions do not persuade me that Mr Sparks’ statements should be excluded. The Court may refuse to admit evidence under s 135 if its probative value is substantially outweighed by the danger that the evidence might (amongst other things) be unfairly prejudicial to a party. BlueScope did not address the probative value of the statements, but in my view the statements have significant probative value. In the relevant period (the second half of 2013 and the first half of 2014), Mr Sparks held the position of National Account Manager & Sales Manager for SA/NT within BlueScope’s Distribution Markets Team, having responsibility for managing BlueScope's national distribution account with Southern Steel. At the time of making his primary statement, Mr Sparks had become the Victorian State Manager for Distribution Markets for BlueScope. Mr Sparks’ statement describes BlueScope’s business and its commercial strategy under Mr Ellis in the relevant period. It follows that I would only exclude Mr Sparks’ statements if persuaded that their probative value is substantially outweighed by the danger that the evidence might be unfairly prejudicial to BlueScope.

In my view, the matters raised by BlueScope do not constitute unfair prejudice. The tender of Mr Sparks’ statements as admissions cannot be regarded as unusual. It is no different to the tender of a written confession in a criminal trial. Mr Sparks remains an employee of BlueScope and it is open to BlueScope to call Mr Sparks as a witness. If Mr Sparks believes that his statements are incorrect, he is able to give evidence and explain how that came about, whether through some unfairness or confusion at the time the statements were taken or because his recollection of relevant events has changed. In circumstances where BlueScope is able to confer with Mr Sparks before he gives evidence, there is no unfair prejudice arising from the fact that BlueScope would be subject to the rules relating to examination-in-chief, including the rule that prevents leading questions. In any event, the Court has power to adjust the rules relating to examination-in-chief if warranted by the circumstances including those specified in s 192(2) of the Evidence Act (which are mandatory considerations: Stanoevski v The Queen (2001) 202 CLR 115 at [41] per Gaudron, Kirby and Callinan JJ). That includes allowing leading questions under s 37(1)(a) or allowing cross-examination on evidence given by the witness that is unfavourable to the calling party under s 38.

Joseph Calleja is the managing director of Apex Steel which, amongst other things, is a distributor of flat steel products. Apex Steel acquires a large proportion of its steel requirements from BlueScope. In the course of its investigation of the conduct which is the subject of this proceeding, the ACCC took a written statement from Mr Calleja, which Mr Calleja signed as true and correct on 29 May 2018. The written statement describes the business of Apex Steel and its competitors (at paragraphs 9 to 18) and certain communications and dealings between BlueScope and Apex Steel which the ACCC alleges constitute an attempt by BlueScope and Mr Ellis to induce Apex Steel to make an arrangement or arrive at an understanding that contains a cartel provision. Relevantly, the statement recorded Mr Calleja’s recollection of:
(a) statements made at a meeting that occurred on 6 September 2013 at the Parkroyal Hotel at Melbourne Airport between Messrs Ellis and Hennessy of BlueScope, Mr Calleja (representing Apex Steel) and a representative of each of Southern Steel, Vulcan Steel and Selection Steel (at paragraphs 19 to 32);
(b) the receipt by Apex Steel of a BlueScope pricing document on 17 September 2013 and associated communications (at paragraphs 33 to 36); and
(c) phone calls received by Mr Calleja from Mr Ellis from October 2013 and throughout 2014 (at paragraphs 37 and 38).

Mr Calleja was an unwilling witness for the ACCC. The ACCC issued a subpoena compelling Mr Calleja’s attendance at the trial to give evidence. Mr Calleja attended the hearing to give evidence on 14 September 2021 in response to the subpoena.

During the course of Mr Calleja’s testimony, I gave leave to the ACCC to ask leading questions of Mr Calleja concerning parts of his statement, a course which was objected to by the respondents. At the conclusion of Mr Calleja’s testimony, the ACCC tendered Mr Calleja’s written statement and the respondents objected to the tender. I reserved my ruling on the admissibility of that part of Mr Calleja’s testimony that involved the leading questions and Mr Calleja’s written statement, and gave the parties the opportunity to file short submissions on that question. Each of the parties filed submissions.

Some further background should be noted. During the trial, the ACCC has called a number of witnesses who had previously given signed written statements to the ACCC. Sections 37(3) and 64(4) of the Evidence Act enable the Court to receive a written statement of a witness as the evidence-in-chief of the witness where the witness affirms the truth of the statement in oral testimony. As Weinberg J observed in Platcher v Joseph [2004] FCAFC 68, the approach of calling a witness to adopt a previous statement as true and correct is routinely followed in the Federal Court (at [163]). It is also permissible for a witness to confirm the truth and accuracy of a prior statement on affidavit: see Alfred v Lanscar (2007) 162 FCR 169; Temple v Powell (No 1) [2007] FCA 987; 164 IR 409 (Temple v Powell (No 1)) at [17]-[22]; Australian Competition and Consumer Commission v Australian Institute of Professional Education Pty Ltd (In Liq) (No 2) [2018] FCA 1459 at [17]-[18] per Bromwich J. However, at the request of the respondents, the ACCC agreed not to tender those parts of the written statements of the witnesses that dealt with oral conversations in issue in the proceeding but to lead such evidence from the witnesses during oral testimony. That is a practice that is commonly followed, particularly in cases such as the present involving allegations of unlawful conduct where civil penalties may be imposed. In Temple v Powell (No 1), French J refused to allow evidence of contested oral conversations contained in examination transcripts and witness statements to be tendered and required this evidence to be adduced orally. His Honour explained (at [25]-[26]):
There is a general and legitimate concern that the liability of the respondents in this case will depend critically upon what the first and third respondents are found to have said prior to the two instances of industrial action complained of in the statement of claim. Generally speaking courts should take a cautious approach before allowing evidence of critical oral conversations to be received, over objection, by way of affidavits or witness statements particularly where the proceedings involve, as in this case, the potential imposition of civil penalties. The presentation of affidavits or witness statements of oral conversations does not disclose the extent to which they have been adduced as a result of leading questions or suggestions put to the deponent. This, of course, does not prevent the adducing of affidavit evidence as to non-critical or uncontentious oral conversations or matters which set out a chronology of events or bring in documentary evidence. These contending considerations can be resolved by allowing the filing of affidavits which cover other matters including chronology, documentation and essentially non-contentious issues but leave the detail of evidence about the content of critical oral conversations to be adduced orally in chief. In my opinion that is the proper course to be taken here.
I propose to direct that evidence-in-chief be on affidavit provided that oral statements said to have been made by the first and third respondents or oral conversations to which they were parties be adduced in chief by oral testimony in the usual way. The timing and location of such oral statements or conversations and their subject matter may be outlined in the affidavit evidence as part of the chronology of events which it covers. The witness may then be invited to give oral evidence as to the particulars of the conversations whose existence and subject nature is disclosed as part of the chronology of events covered by the affidavits.

In the present case, Mr Calleja’s witness statement was a formal statement that had been signed as true and correct by Mr Calleja on 29 March 2018, some 5 years after the events referred to in the statement occurred, but more than 3 years prior to the trial. As noted above, Mr Calleja was an unwilling witness and attended the trial to give evidence in response to a subpoena issued by the ACCC. In those circumstances, and in light of the evidence given by Mr Calleja (discussed further below), I infer that the ACCC had been unable to confer with Mr Calleja in recent times. He was available to be cross-examined by the respondents. This may have been a case in which the Court would have permitted the ACCC to tender Mr Calleja’s written statement as his evidence-in-chief if it was affirmed as true and correct by Mr Calleja, without requiring evidence of contentious conversations to be adduced in vive voce in examination-in-chief.

The ACCC did not, however, adopt that course in respect of Mr Calleja’s evidence. The ACCC informed the Court and the respondents that it proposed to ask Mr Calleja questions to confirm that he had given a written statement and to affirm its truth, ask non-leading questions of Mr Calleja about his current recollection in relation to the matters covered by paragraphs 19 to 38 of his statement, and then seek to tender the whole of Mr Calleja’s statement. The course adopted led to difficulties.

Early in his examination-in-chief by the ACCC, Mr Calleja confirmed that he had given a written statement to the ACCC, that he had read the statement recently and that the statement was true and correct to the best of his knowledge and belief. Counsel for the ACCC then proceeded to ask non-leading questions of Mr Calleja about the matters addressed at paragraphs 19 to 38 of the written statement.

In relation to the meeting on 6 September 2013, Mr Calleja gave evidence to the effect that Mr Ellis arranged the meeting, that the meeting occurred and identified the attendees, that Mr Ellis did most of the speaking, that Mr Ellis said that BlueScope would be issuing a new price list which would contain recommended retail prices and that either Mr Ellis or Mr Hennessy may have told Mr Calleja to keep the meeting quiet. Most of the evidence given by Mr Calleja was uncontroversial (apart, perhaps, from the request to keep the meeting quiet). Mr Calleja was pressed as to whether he could recall anything else said by Mr Ellis at the meeting, and he said that he did not. That answer was significant because Mr Calleja’s written statement (at paragraph 27) contained further details of statements purportedly made by Mr Ellis at the meeting about the use of the recommended price list including that BlueScope was going to increase the prices that it charged BlueScope’s own distribution arms, that there was an opportunity for all distributors to achieve better profit margins by increasing prices, that Mr Ellis intended to implement an initiative whereby BlueScope would set recommended retail prices, and that BlueScope would send a price list containing recommended retail prices to distributors and distributors could use those prices to benchmark their prices for steel products.

In relation to the receipt by Apex Steel of the BlueScope price list on 17 September 2013, Mr Calleja said that Mr Hennessy may have called him before the document was sent but he could not remember any specific conversations. Mr Calleja also said that Mr Hennessy may have called him after the price list was sent, but Mr Calleja could not recall the conversation and believed that Mr Hennessy would have asked him whether he had received the document and Mr Calleja would have said that he would forward the document to the person who does the purchasing (of steel products). Again those answers were significant because Mr Calleja’s written statement (at paragraph 34) contained further details of statements purportedly made by Mr Hennessy to Mr Calleja before the price list was sent to the effect that the price list included recommended retail prices spoken about by Mr Ellis at the meeting on 6 September 2013 and that Mr Hennessy encouraged Mr Calleja to implement the recommended prices and increase Apex Steel’s prices.

In relation to phone calls received by Mr Calleja from Mr Ellis from October 2013 and throughout 2014, Mr Calleja said that he received a few phone calls over that period and Mr Ellis asked him to get Nello Campagnino (who was responsible for purchasing steel products at Apex Steel) to buy more steel from BlueScope. Mr Calleja said that he did not recall any other aspect of Mr Ellis’ phone calls. Again those answers were significant because Mr Calleja’s written statement (at paragraph 37) contained further details of statements purportedly made by Mr Ellis to Mr Calleja putting pressure on Mr Calleja to increase Apex Steel’s prices for the sale of steel products.

At that point, counsel for the ACCC tendered Mr Calleja’s statement under either s 37(3) or s 64(4) of the Evidence Act. I heard objections to the tender and argument in the absence of Mr Calleja. The respondents objected to the tender of the whole of the statement, largely on the basis that Mr Calleja had given oral testimony as to the matters that were the subject of paragraphs 19 to 36 of his statement. I informed counsel for the ACCC that I could not be satisfied that Mr Calleja had affirmed and adopted the written statement as being true and correct, by reason of the subsequent evidence he had given to the effect that he could not recall significant matters that were addressed in the written statement. I indicated that I would find it difficult to receive the written statement as evidence unless Mr Calleja was taken to precise parts of the statement and asked whether he believed that the matters recorded in the statement were correct. Counsel for the respondents opposed that course principally on the basis that it would offend the rule against leading questions. I nevertheless gave the ACCC leave to ask questions about the contents of the written statement (which would necessarily be in a leading form) prior to any cross-examination, and indicated that I would reserve any ruling on the admissibility of the written statement and the further questions and answers given by Mr Calleja.

In accordance with the leave I granted (which was to ask leading questions within a limited scope relating to Mr Calleja’s statement), counsel for the ACCC took Mr Calleja to specific passages in his written statement between paragraphs 19 to 36 and asked him whether, when he signed the statement, he believed what was recorded to be true and correct, whether he now believed that what was recorded was true and correct and whether he now had a recollection of the matters recorded. Mr Calleja’s evidence was to the effect that he could not recall his state of mind in 2018, but he was certain that what he signed in 2018 was correct. Significantly, in respect of a number of the paragraphs that Mr Calleja was taken to (including paragraphs 27, 34 and 37 referred to above), Mr Calleja gave evidence that he now recalled the matters set out in the statement. At the conclusion of those questions, counsel for the ACCC renewed the tender of the written statement. I reserved my decision on the receipt of the written statement and the further oral testimony of Mr Calleja. The respondents were content to cross-examine Mr Calleja prior to a ruling being made.
However, it was not put to Mr Calleja that the conversations recounted in the statement were suggested to him or that he was pressured in any way to agree to the statement.

In further cross-examination, it was put to Mr Calleja that it was possible that different words were spoken, and that he could not be sure of the words spoken, in the key conversations referred to above. Mr Calleja generally agreed with what was put to him. That evidence was not inconsistent with his earlier evidence. A witness can believe that a conversation occurred in a particular form, but might not be wholly sure of the words spoken and concede the possibility that different words were used. However, as cross-examination proceeded, Mr Calleja reverted to stating that he could not recall the key conversations.
The question that arises for determination is whether the leading questions asked of Mr Calleja by the ACCC (with leave of the Court), and his written statement, should be admitted in evidence.

BlueScope maintained its objection to the parts of Mr Calleja’s written statement on which the ACCC asked leading questions (paragraphs 19 to 36) and Mr Calleja’s testimony in response to those questions. BlueScope’s objection did not apply to paragraphs 1 to 18 of Mr Calleja’s statement (which were not the subject of the further questions during examination-in-chief) or paragraph 34 (on which Mr Calleja was cross-examined). BlueScope submitted that the course that was adopted in examination-in-chief had the result that the written statement constituted inconsistent and contradictory evidence of the evidence given orally. As a result, neither the witness statement (nor the leading questions and answers that resulted from its use) would be evidence that would be admitted pursuant to s 37 of the Evidence Act, and it is evidence of the sort that would attract the prohibition in s 32. BlueScope further submitted that, if the statement was otherwise admissible pursuant to s 64(4), the Court should exclude it pursuant to s 135, and that exclusion would apply to the oral evidence given with the use of the statement. In that respect, BlueScope argued that it would be unfairly prejudicial to BlueScope to permit the ACCC to adduce two inconsistent versions of Mr Calleja’s evidence, the ACCC having agreed that the relevant evidence would be given orally (and having adduced such evidence), and this outweighs the probative value of the written statement, especially given the extent of disavowal of the evidence by Mr Calleja in the course of his oral evidence. The evidence would also be misleading and confusing. If the Court were to receive the evidence, the Court would be left with two inconsistent, but incomplete, versions without a proper means for resolving or testing the inconsistency. This was only exacerbated by Mr Calleja’s responses in cross-examination which, despite the apparent effect of his review of his statement in refreshing his memory, revealed that those recollections were likely incorrect, or certainly could not be said to be correct.

Mr Ellis similarly submitted that both the written statement and the associated examination-in-chief should not be received into evidence. Indeed, Mr Ellis went further than BlueScope and submitted that the written statement should be rejected in its entirety. Mr Ellis argued that the evidence is not relevant, as it is incapable of rationally affecting the assessment of the probability of the existence of any fact in issue. If the Court were to conclude that the evidence satisfies the relevance threshold, the evidence should be excluded under s 135 on the basis of the danger that the evidence might be either unfairly prejudicial, or alternatively misleading or confusing. Mr Ellis argued that the only way in which the written statement and associated examination-in-chief could have any probative value in relation to the issues arising in these proceedings would be if Mr Calleja had a superior recall of the matters in his statement, but his testimony does not establish that proposition. Mr Ellis also submitted that the evidence would be misleading or confusing because, having regard to the whole of Mr Calleja’s evidence, there is a real danger of the Court being misled if any weight were attached to the evidence.

The ACCC submitted that the matters raised by the respondents (inconsistencies between Mr Calleja’s oral evidence-in-chief, his written statement and his cross-examination) do not go to admissibility but concern the reliability of Mr Calleja’s evidence. The ACCC submitted that the written statement is admissible under ss 37(3) and 64(4) of the Evidence Act. The ACCC did not seek leave under s 32 and no reliance was placed on that section. The ACCC further submitted that there was no occasion to exclude the evidence under s 135. Mr Calleja’s written statement has significant probative value. The unfair prejudice to which s 135(a) is addressed is the danger that the fact-finder may use the evidence to make a decision on an improper or unacceptable basis, for example by the evidence provoking some irrational, emotional or illogical response, or by giving it more weight than it deserves (referring to R v Suteski (2002) 56 NSWLR 182 at [116] per Wood CJ at CL with whom Sully and Howie JJ agreed). The ACCC submitted that there is no risk of such unfair prejudice arising in respect of Mr Calleja’s evidence. The Court is able to consider any inconsistencies in Mr Calleja’s evidence and assess the totality of his evidence in an appropriate way. There is no risk of the Court being misled or confused merely because there are inconsistencies in Mr Calleja’s evidence.
In my view, the leading questions asked of Mr Calleja by the ACCC (with leave of the Court), and his written statement, should be admitted into evidence largely for the reasons submitted by the ACCC.

The course of examination-in-chief of Mr Calleja, involving the use of leading questions with respect to his written statement, was unusual. I gave leave to the ACCC to ask such leading questions, without taking the formal step of declaring the witness hostile (unfavourable under s 38 of the Evidence Act) because, at the time that the ACCC first tendered the written statement, I was left in doubt whether Mr Calleja had affirmed and adopted the statement. As the ACCC submitted during the hearing, further questions on the statement may have led to the conclusion that the witness was indeed hostile. Instead, Mr Calleja affirmed the contents of his written statement. A similar (but not identical) course was permitted by Dixon J in R v Neal (1947) 53 ALR (CN) 616a, which was considered by the Full Court of the Supreme Court in R v Thynne [1977] VR 98. The Full Court described the approach adopted by Dixon J as follows (at 101):
During the course of the prosecution case, a witness for the prosecution gave evasive answers and professed himself unable to recollect certain events. On an application by counsel for the prosecution to have the witness declared hostile and for permission to cross-examine him generally, Dixon, J., without determining whether the witness was "hostile", gave leave to counsel for the prosecution to cross-examine the witness by leading questions in conformity with the terms of the written statement made by the witness in the course of the preparation for the trial. That leave was limited to cross-examination as to the facts recorded in the statement in writing. There was no leave to cross-examine the witness generally. Dixon, J., reserving to counsel the right to make application at a later stage for leave to cross-examine generally if it should then appear that the witness was "hostile" in the relevant sense ...

The Full Court noted that the leading questions permitted by Dixon J were directed to the facts stated in the witness statement (which was in the hands of the witness), not to proof that the witness had made the written statement (at 102).

On their terms, ss 37 and 64 of the Evidence Act allow the Court to receive into evidence a prior written statement of the witness as evidence of the facts stated in the statement: see J D Heydon, Cross on Evidence (12th ed, LexisNexis Australia, 2000) Ch 9 “The Course of Evidence” at [17320]. It would seem to be implicit in s 37(3) that the Court would only permit a written statement to be tendered as the evidence-in-chief of the maker if the statement were affirmed by the maker on affidavit or by oral testimony, enabling the maker to be cross-examined on the statement. Similarly, in Osborne Metal Industries (NSW) Pty Ltd v Bullock (No 1) [2011] NSWSC 636, McDougall J considered that the exception to the hearsay rule in s 64(3) is predicated upon the ability of the party against whom the document is tendered to cross-examine the person about the representations in the document (at [26]).

In the present case, I consider that Mr Calleja affirmed the facts stated in his written statement during examination-in-chief. He did so twice: at the commencement of his testimony and subsequently in response to leading questions asked with leave of the Court. The circumstance that his evidence was inconsistent, and that his second affirmation resulted from leading questions, affects the credibility of his evidence (including his written statement), but not, in my view, its admissibility. The further inconsistent evidence given by Mr Calleja during cross-examination also affects the credibility of his evidence but not, in my view, its admissibility.

I am not persuaded that the probative value of the objected to evidence (the written statement and the leading questions and answers) is substantially outweighed by the danger that the evidence might be unfairly prejudicial to a party or be misleading or confusing. The respondents were able to cross-examine Mr Calleja. The respondents did not submit that they were unable to do so effectively. The parties will be able to make submissions with respect to the weight, if any, to be given to Mr Calleja’s written statement in the course of closing submissions.

For those reasons, I allow the tender of Mr Calleja’s written statement and that part of his examination-in-chief which comprised the leading questions asked of Mr Calleja by the ACCC and Mr Calleja’s answers.
